summary: A report showing how the requirements for advancing BGP-4 to Draft Standard were met. It satisfies the second report required by RFC 1264, augments RFC 1774, and summarizes key features of BGP-4. It also analyzes the protocol with respect to scaling and performance. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card for a routing protocol, showing it passed the tests needed to move up a grade.

subtitle: How BGP-4 meets the requirements to be an Internet routing standard

tldr.problem: The IETF needed verification that BGP-4 satisfied the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard status.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4274 analyzes BGP-4's key features, algorithms, scalability, performance, and policy expressiveness against the criteria in RFC 1264, fulfilling the required 'second report' for Draft Standard advancement.
tldr.outcome: BGP-4 was confirmed as an Internet Standard for inter-autonomous system routing. The analysis also documents important limitations: policy configurations can lead to route oscillations and non-deterministic routing.

today: RFC 4274 is an informational document that analyzed BGP-4 to meet RFC 1264 requirements for Draft Standard. BGP-4 is now an Internet Standard (RFC 4271) and remains the primary inter-autonomous system routing protocol used across the internet.

sections.title: BGP and Its Evolution
sections.content: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the inter-autonomous system routing protocol used across the modern internet. Earlier versions (BGP-1 through BGP-3) lacked support for Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) and became obsolete. BGP-4 was developed to support CIDR and is documented in RFC 4271. This report documents how BGP-4 satisfies the requirements in RFC 1264 for publication as a Draft Standard. It fulfills the requirement for the 'second report', augments RFC 1774 (an earlier BGP-4 analysis), and analyzes BGP-4's scaling and performance characteristics.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP is a language routers use to tell each other which paths they know about for reaching different parts of the internet. BGP-4 is the current version and this document checks whether it is good enough to be official.

sections.title: Key Features and Algorithms
sections.content: BGP is designed for routing between multiple autonomous systems (ASes). It assumes that routing within each AS is handled by interior gateway protocols (IGPs). The protocol uses a path vector algorithm, which pairs destination information with path information to avoid the distance vector problems of earlier protocols. Each route includes AS_PATH information, a list of autonomous systems the route has traversed, which enables straightforward loop detection and powerful policy-based routing. BGP also supports route aggregation so that groups of destinations using hierarchical address assignment (like CIDR) can be summarized into single announcements, reducing the routing table size. BGP maintains only one connection per peer at steady state and uses TCP port 179 for reliability. The BGP Finite State Machine manages peer connections through states including IDLE, CONNECT, ACTIVE, OPENSENT, OPENCONFIRM, and ESTABLISHED.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP keeps track of the path to each destination so it doesn't loop back on itself. It groups many small route announcements into bigger ones to save space and bandwidth.

sections.title: Scalability and Performance
sections.content: BGP's bandwidth and CPU consumption depend heavily on network stability. When the network is stable, routers exchange only KEEPALIVE messages every 30 seconds (about 19 octets, consuming roughly 5 bits per second). During instability, UPDATE messages carry routing changes. The worst-case bandwidth for initial exchange between peers is O((N + A) * P), where N is the total number of routes, A is total path attributes, and P is the number of peers. At the time of writing, the full set of exterior routes in BGP was approximately 134,000 entries. Memory requirements scale linearly with the total number of networks multiplied by the number of peers. Router BGP RIB tables typically carry around 120,000 entries, with room to scale to 1,000,000 entries in robust implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: When things are quiet, BGP uses barely any internet bandwidth. When lots of routes change at once, it uses more. Routers can remember tens of thousands of routes easily.

sections.title: Policy Expressiveness and Its Limitations
sections.content: BGP is unique among deployed routing protocols in using semantically rich routing policies to determine which paths to use. Vendors implement policy languages with hundreds of commands, and these languages are not standardized in the RFC. This flexibility has enabled creative network engineering but has exposed a fundamental limitation: locally defined policies can interact in unexpected ways. The RFC documents two important cases. First, it is possible to construct policies where multiple stable routing solutions exist, with BGP having no way to prefer the intended solution. Second, policies can be constructed that lead to route oscillations, where BGP never finds a stable state. These issues arise from the unconstrained nature of policy languages and are unlikely to become less common as policies grow more complex.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks use complicated rules to decide which path to use for sending traffic. Sometimes these rules conflict with each other and the router keeps changing its mind about the best path.

sections.title: Applicability and Implementation
sections.content: BGP is well suited for routing between autonomous systems that use IP and the hop-by-hop routing paradigm. The protocol contains only essential functionality while providing mechanisms for extension. BGP capabilities (RFC 3392) provide a flexible way to introduce new features. Implementation guidelines recommend that robust BGP implementations be work-conserving (tolerating arbitrarily high route flap rates without losing peerings), isolate instability to affected prefixes, and bound the impact of unstable peers on convergence time for stable routes. Numerous robust implementations exist, demonstrating that producing a correct implementation is achievable, though not trivial.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP works well for connecting internet providers and large networks to each other, especially because it can be extended with new features when needed.
